A simple improvement on Kerman’s approximation
to the median of the beta distribution

Richard F. Lyon Affiliation: Google Research, Mountain View, California, USA Email: dicklyon@acm.org
October 24, 2026
Abstract

Kerman’s approximation to the median of the Beta⁡(α,β)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) distribution is the ratio g⁡(α)/(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)) with g⁡(x)=x−13g(x)=x-\frac{1}{3}, using the first two terms of the asymptotic expansion of the median of the standard gamma distribution. We extend this elegant ratio form to the one-parameter family with g⁡(x)=x−13+c1/xg(x)=x-\frac{1}{3}+c_{1}/x, in which c1=0c_{1}=0 gives Kerman’s. For large shape parameters along any ray β=r​α\beta=r\alpha with r>1r>1, the resulting approximation is eventually a lower bound on the median if c1≤8405c_{1}\leq\frac{8}{405} and an upper bound if c1≥145c_{1}\geq\frac{1}{45}. We recommend c1=136c_{1}=\frac{1}{36} for its simplicity: it makes g⁡(x)=(x−16)2/xg(x)=(x-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/x a perfect square over xx, and it is within 1%1\% of the minimax value of c1c_{1} for α,β≥1\alpha,\beta\geq 1 under several error measures, while the theoretically distinguished values 8405\frac{8}{405} and 145\frac{1}{45} are less accurate. The approximation is then

ν1/36​(α,β)=(α−16)2/α(α−16)2/α+(β−16)2/β.\nu_{1/36}(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/\alpha}{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/\alpha+(\beta-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/\beta}\,.

Its relative error lies between −0.171%-0.171\% and +0.212%+0.212\% for all 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta, compared with up to −3.8%-3.8\% for Kerman’s. It is more accurate than Kerman’s approximation wherever the latter is defined, with relative error never more than 1332\frac{13}{32} of Kerman’s, the ratio approached asymptotically. The same g⁡(α)g(\alpha) is a useful approximation to the gamma distribution median, overestimating it by at most 0.212%0.212\% for shape parameter α≥1\alpha\geq 1.

Keywords: approximation, asymptotic expansion, beta distribution, gamma distribution, median, posterior median

1 Introduction

The median νB​(α,β)\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta) of the beta distribution with shape parameters α\alpha and β\beta, the solution xx of Ix​(α,β)=12I_{x}(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{1}{2}, has no closed form except in special cases. Simple approximations to it are useful because it comes up often: it is the posterior median of a binomial proportion under a conjugate beta prior, such as the neutral prior Beta⁡(13,13)\mathrm{Beta}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3}) of Kerman, 2011b (), whose posteriors have both shape parameters at least 13\frac{1}{3}; it is the median of the kkth order statistic of a uniform sample of size nn, which has the Beta⁡(k,n−k+1)\mathrm{Beta}(k,n-k+1) distribution, and so gives the median ranks used in probability plotting; and it is a natural starting value for the numerical inversion of IxI_{x}.

Kerman, 2011a () proposed the approximation

νB​(α,β)≈α−13α+β−23,\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta)\approx\frac{\alpha-\frac{1}{3}}{\alpha+\beta-\frac{2}{3}}\,, (1)

which is asymptotically accurate as both shape parameters grow. It has the ratio form g⁡(α)/(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)) with g⁡(x)=x−13g(x)=x-\frac{1}{3}. We study the one-parameter family

gc1​(x)=x−13+c1x,νc1​(α,β)=gc1​(α)gc1​(α)+gc1​(β),g_{c_{1}}(x)=x-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{c_{1}}{x}\,,\qquad\nu_{c_{1}}(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{g_{c_{1}}(\alpha)}{g_{c_{1}}(\alpha)+g_{c_{1}}(\beta)}\,, (2)

with c1≥0c_{1}\geq 0, in which c1=0c_{1}=0 gives Kerman’s approximation. Our recommended member has c1=136c_{1}=\frac{1}{36}, for which gg factors as g1/36​(x)=(x−16)2/xg_{1/36}(x)=(x-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/x, and ν1/36\nu_{1/36} can be written in several forms:

ν1/36​(α,β)=g1/36​(α)g1/36​(α)+g1/36​(β)=(α−16)2/α(α−16)2/α+(β−16)2/β=α−13+136​αα+β−23+136​α+136​β=(α−16)2​β(α−16)2​β+(β−16)2​α=(6​α−1)2​β(6​α−1)2​β+(6​β−1)2​α.\begin{split}\nu_{1/36}(\alpha,\beta)&=\frac{g_{1/36}(\alpha)}{g_{1/36}(\alpha)+g_{1/36}(\beta)}=\frac{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/\alpha}{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/\alpha+(\beta-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/\beta}\\[4.0pt] &=\frac{\alpha-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{36\alpha}}{\alpha+\beta-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{36\alpha}+\frac{1}{36\beta}}\\[4.0pt] &=\frac{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}\,\beta}{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}\,\beta+(\beta-\frac{1}{6})^{2}\,\alpha}=\frac{(6\alpha-1)^{2}\,\beta}{(6\alpha-1)^{2}\,\beta+(6\beta-1)^{2}\,\alpha}\,.\end{split} (3)

It is nearly as simple as Kerman’s approximation but much more accurate: over 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta its relative error is at most 0.212%0.212\%, against 3.82%3.82\% for Kerman’s, and 136≈0.027778\frac{1}{36}\approx 0.027778 is within 1%1\% of the minimax value of c1c_{1} there, 0.0275370.027537, whose worst error is 0.189%0.189\%. Since g1/36g_{1/36} has a double zero at x=16x=\frac{1}{6} and grows again below it, ν1/36\nu_{1/36} is intended for α,β>16\alpha,\beta>\frac{1}{6}; it is most accurate for α,β≥1\alpha,\beta\geq 1, and its relative error stays within 3.3%3.3\% for α,β≥12\alpha,\beta\geq\frac{1}{2} and 14.4%14.4\% for α,β≥13\alpha,\beta\geq\frac{1}{3} (Table 1).

Section 2 reviews the properties of ratio forms, the gamma median expansion behind them, and two older approximations of the same kind. Section 3 locates ν1/36\nu_{1/36} within the family by its asymptotic behavior for large shape parameters. Section 4 compares its accuracy with Kerman’s and other members numerically. Section 5 maps the value of c1c_{1} that would make the ratio form exact at each (α,β)(\alpha,\beta). Section 6 discusses minimax and shape-dependent choices of c1c_{1}. Finally, Section 7 briefly explores corresponding approximations to the gamma median.

2 Background and related approximations

Every ratio form is exact on the diagonal α=β\alpha=\beta of the (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) plane, where the median is 12\frac{1}{2}, and respects the symmetry νB​(β,α)=1−νB​(α,β)\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\beta,\alpha)=1-\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta). When β\beta is large, the beta distribution approaches a gamma distribution scaled by 1/β1/\beta, so β​νB​(α,β)→νΓ​(α)\beta\,\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta)\to\nu_{\Gamma}(\alpha), the median of the gamma distribution with shape parameter α\alpha and unit scale; a ratio form with g⁡(x)∼xg(x)\sim x correspondingly has β​g​(α)/(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))→g⁡(α)\beta\,g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(\beta))\to g(\alpha). So a good gamma median approximation gg makes a good beta median approximation at large β\beta. The gamma median has no closed form either, but it has a well-known asymptotic expansion (Choi,, 1994; Berg and Pedersen,, 2006),

νΓ​(α)=α−13+8405​α+18425515​α2+⋯,\nu_{\Gamma}(\alpha)=\alpha-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{8}{405\alpha}+\frac{184}{25515\alpha^{2}}+\cdots\,, (4)

and α−13\alpha-\frac{1}{3} is a lower bound on it (Chen and Rubin,, 1986; Berg and Pedersen,, 2006). Kerman’s gg consists of the first two terms of (4), and truncating after the third term gives ν8/405\nu_{8/405}.

An older ratio form is implicit in the normal approximation to the FF distribution of Paulson, (1942), which applies the cube-root transformation of Wilson and Hilferty, (1931) to the numerator and denominator of FF. Setting Paulson’s normal deviate to zero gives the median of FF with n1n_{1} and n2n_{2} degrees of freedom as ((1−29​n1)/(1−29​n2))3\big((1-\frac{2}{9n_{1}})/(1-\frac{2}{9n_{2}})\big)^{3}. Since α​F/(α​F+β)\alpha F/(\alpha F+\beta) has the Beta⁡(α,β)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) distribution when n1=2​αn_{1}=2\alpha and n2=2​βn_{2}=2\beta, this is the ratio form with

gWH​(x)=x​(1−19​x)3=x−13+127​x−1729​x2.g_{\mathrm{WH}}(x)=x\Big(1-\frac{1}{9x}\Big)^{3}=x-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{27x}-\frac{1}{729x^{2}}\,.

The resulting νWH\nu_{\mathrm{WH}} is already more accurate than Kerman’s approximation: over 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta it overestimates the median by at most 1.33%1.33\%, where Kerman’s underestimates it by up to 3.82%3.82\%, and it is better on every domain of Table 1. But it is little known as an approximation to the beta median, since it appears only implicitly, as the median case of an approximation to the FF distribution. Kerman’s gg, gWHg_{\mathrm{WH}} and the series (4) all have the form x−13+c1/x+c2/x2+⋯x-\frac{1}{3}+c_{1}/x+c_{2}/x^{2}+\cdots: Kerman’s with c1=c2=0c_{1}=c_{2}=0, gWHg_{\mathrm{WH}} with c1=127=15405c_{1}=\frac{1}{27}=\frac{15}{405} and c2=−1729c_{2}=-\frac{1}{729}, and the series with c1=8405c_{1}=\frac{8}{405} and c2=18425515c_{2}=\frac{184}{25515}. Section 3 shows that for large shape parameters only c1c_{1} matters to second order, which is why we concentrate on the family (2).

Approximations to percentage points of Fisher’s z=12​log⁡Fz=\frac{1}{2}\log F also give the beta median, but they are designed for the tails. At the median, Carter,’s (1947) refinement of the Fisher–Cochran formula reduces to logit⁡ν=log⁡(α/β)−23​(u−v)​(1−u−v)\logit\nu=\log(\alpha/\beta)-\frac{2}{3}(u-v)(1-u-v), with u=1/(2​α−1)u=1/(2\alpha-1) and v=1/(2​β−1)v=1/(2\beta-1). It is singular at α\alpha or β=12\beta=\frac{1}{2}, and to second order its logit matches that of a ratio form with c1=118c_{1}=\frac{1}{18}; over 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta its worst relative error is +44%+44\%, at α=1\alpha=1 as β→∞\beta\to\infty, where it gives 1/β1/\beta in place of (log⁡2)/β(\log 2)/\beta.

3 Asymptotic bounds along rays

When both shape parameters are large, every member of the family (2) agrees with the median to first order in 1/α1/\alpha; the members differ at second order, where c1c_{1} alone decides whether the approximation lies above or below the median. Along each ray β=r​α\beta=r\alpha with r>1r>1, the dividing value of c1c_{1} is explicit. The two theorems below are proved in Appendix A.

Theorem 1 (Asymptotic bounds).

Fix r>1r>1 and let

cr∗=8405+4​r405​(1+r)2.c^{*}_{r}=\frac{8}{405}+\frac{4r}{405\,(1+r)^{2}}\,.

Let g⁡(x)=x−13+c1/x+O⁡(x−2)g(x)=x-\frac{1}{3}+c_{1}/x+O(x^{-2}) as x→∞x\to\infty. If c1<cr∗c_{1}<c^{*}_{r}, then g⁡(α)/(g⁡(α)+g⁡(r​α))<νB​(α,r​α)g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(r\alpha))<\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,r\alpha) for all sufficiently large α\alpha. If c1>cr∗c_{1}>c^{*}_{r}, the reverse inequality holds for all sufficiently large α\alpha.

The threshold has a simple meaning: along each ray, the median itself agrees to second order with the ratio form νcr∗\nu_{c^{*}_{r}}, as (9) in the proof shows. Since 0<4​r/(1+r)2<10<4r/(1+r)^{2}<1 for r>1r>1, we have 8405<cr∗<9405=145\frac{8}{405}<c^{*}_{r}<\frac{9}{405}=\frac{1}{45}. So c1≤8405c_{1}\leq\frac{8}{405} gives an asymptotic lower bound on every ray, c1≥145c_{1}\geq\frac{1}{45} an asymptotic upper bound on every ray, and c1c_{1} strictly between gives one or the other depending on the ray. In particular, Kerman’s ν0\nu_{0}, the truncated series ν8/405\nu_{8/405} and the ratio form of the true gamma median itself are asymptotic lower bounds, while ν1/36\nu_{1/36} is an asymptotic upper bound.

Remark 1.

At c1=145c_{1}=\frac{1}{45} the second-order term vanishes as r→1r\to 1, so near the diagonal the sign is decided at third order. Numerically, c1=145c_{1}=\frac{1}{45} fails to be an upper bound in a thin region near the diagonal (β/α<1.51\beta/\alpha<1.51 at α=100\alpha=100) that shrinks as α\alpha grows.

Theorem 2 (Asymptotic error).

Fix r>1r>1 and c1≥0c_{1}\geq 0. As α→∞\alpha\to\infty with β=r​α\beta=r\alpha, the relative error ec1=νc1/νB−1e_{c_{1}}=\nu_{c_{1}}/\nu_{\mathrm{B}}-1 satisfies

ec1​(α,r​α)=−(1−1r)​cr∗−c1α2+O⁡(α−3).e_{c_{1}}(\alpha,r\alpha)=-\Big(1-\frac{1}{r}\Big)\,\frac{c^{*}_{r}-c_{1}}{\alpha^{2}}+O(\alpha^{-3})\,.

In particular

e1/36e0→−136−cr∗cr∗,\frac{e_{1/36}}{e_{0}}\to-\frac{\frac{1}{36}-c^{*}_{r}}{c^{*}_{r}}\,,

whose magnitude increases from 14\frac{1}{4} as r→1r\to 1 to 1332\frac{13}{32} as r→∞r\to\infty.

For example, along the ray β=2​α\beta=2\alpha, Kerman’s approximation has relative error about −0.0110/α2-0.0110/\alpha^{2} and ν1/36\nu_{1/36} about +0.0029/α2+0.0029/\alpha^{2}.

4 The recommended approximation with c1=136c_{1}=\frac{1}{36}

Figure 1 compares the relative errors of ν1/36\nu_{1/36} and other members of the family for several values of β\beta, and Table 1 gives the worst errors over three domains. On 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta, the relative error of ν1/36\nu_{1/36} lies between −0.171%-0.171\% (near α=1\alpha=1, β≈1.84\beta\approx 1.84) and +0.212%+0.212\% (near α=1.18\alpha=1.18 as β→∞\beta\to\infty), an eighteenth of Kerman’s worst error there.

Comparison with Kerman’s approximation.

The improvement holds pointwise, not only in the worst case. On a grid covering 13<α≤β≤106\frac{1}{3}<\alpha\leq\beta\leq 10^{6}, including points within 10−610^{-6} of the diagonal in β/α\beta/\alpha, the relative error of ν1/36\nu_{1/36} is everywhere smaller in magnitude than that of ν0\nu_{0}, and the ratio of the two stays below 1332=0.40625\frac{13}{32}=0.40625.

Bounds.

Although ν1/36\nu_{1/36} is an asymptotic upper bound on every ray (Section 3), it is not an upper bound everywhere: its negative errors are confined to a region near the diagonal that shrinks as α\alpha grows. The sign of the error just off the diagonal changes at α≈2.059\alpha\approx 2.059, and, numerically on our grid at least, ν1/36≥νB\nu_{1/36}\geq\nu_{\mathrm{B}} throughout 2.06≤α≤β2.06\leq\alpha\leq\beta. Paulson’s νWH\nu_{\mathrm{WH}} is also an asymptotic upper bound on every ray, and on our grid it is an upper bound throughout 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta, but with six times the worst error of ν1/36\nu_{1/36} there.

Smaller shape parameters.

Below α=1\alpha=1 the errors of ν1/36\nu_{1/36} grow, mainly on the negative side (Table 1). Over α,β≥13\alpha,\beta\geq\frac{1}{3}, its relative error is at most 14.4%14.4\% in magnitude, while Kerman’s approximation reaches −100%-100\% at α=13\alpha=\frac{1}{3}, where its gg vanishes; the minimax member for that domain (Section 6) keeps the error within 2.44%2.44\%.

5 The ideal parameter

Setting νc1​(α,β)\nu_{c_{1}}(\alpha,\beta) equal to the median m=νB​(α,β)m=\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta) and solving for c1c_{1} gives the value that makes the ratio form exact at (α,β)(\alpha,\beta),

c∗​(α,β)=m⁡(β−13)−(1−m)​(α−13)(1−m)/α−m/β.c^{*}(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{m\left(\beta-\frac{1}{3}\right)-(1-m)\left(\alpha-\frac{1}{3}\right)}{(1-m)/\alpha-m/\beta}\,. (5)

It is symmetric: c∗​(β,α)=c∗​(α,β)c^{*}(\beta,\alpha)=c^{*}(\alpha,\beta). For α<β\alpha<\beta, the denominator is positive, since m/(1−m)<1<β/αm/(1-m)<1<\beta/\alpha; on the diagonal, where every ratio form is exact, numerator and denominator both vanish and c∗c^{*} is defined by continuity. By l’Hôpital’s rule, with m′=∂m/∂βm^{\prime}=\partial m/\partial\beta at β=α\beta=\alpha,

c∗​(α,α)=α2​(1+4​m′​(α−13))1−4​α​m′.c^{*}(\alpha,\alpha)=\frac{\alpha^{2}\left(1+4m^{\prime}\left(\alpha-\frac{1}{3}\right)\right)}{1-4\alpha\,m^{\prime}}\,.

In general m′m^{\prime} has no closed form, so this does not give c∗c^{*} on the diagonal explicitly. At α=1\alpha=1, however, m=1−2−1/βm=1-2^{-1/\beta} gives m′=−12​log⁡2m^{\prime}=-\frac{1}{2}\log 2, and so

c∗​(1,1)=3−4​log⁡23​(1+2​log⁡2)≈0.03177.c^{*}(1,1)=\frac{3-4\log 2}{3\,(1+2\log 2)}\approx 0.03177\,.

Elsewhere on and near the diagonal, where (5) loses accuracy to cancellation, the notebook evaluates c∗c^{*} at a nearby pair symmetric about it. By the proof of Theorem 1, c∗​(α,r​α)→cr∗c^{*}(\alpha,r\alpha)\to c^{*}_{r} as α→∞\alpha\to\infty along each ray.

Where α\alpha and β\beta both exceed 16\frac{1}{6}, and gc1g_{c_{1}} is positive at both, νc1​(α,β)\nu_{c_{1}}(\alpha,\beta) increases with c1c_{1} for α<β\alpha<\beta: the derivative of log⁡(gc1​(α)/gc1​(β))\log\big(g_{c_{1}}(\alpha)/g_{c_{1}}(\beta)\big) with respect to c1c_{1} is 1/(α​gc1​(α))−1/(β​gc1​(β))1/(\alpha g_{c_{1}}(\alpha))-1/(\beta g_{c_{1}}(\beta)), and x​gc1​(x)=x2−x/3+c1x\,g_{c_{1}}(x)=x^{2}-x/3+c_{1} increases for x>16x>\frac{1}{6}. In that region, then, the contour c∗=c1c^{*}=c_{1} is the curve on which νc1\nu_{c_{1}} is exact, and νc1\nu_{c_{1}} overestimates the median where c∗<c1c^{*}<c_{1} and underestimates it where c∗>c1c^{*}>c_{1}.

Figure 2 shows contours of c∗c^{*} on arctan\arctan axes covering [0,∞]2[0,\infty]^{2}. Numerically, c∗c^{*} has a single peak, on the diagonal: c∗≈0.03440c^{*}\approx 0.03440 at α=β≈0.468\alpha=\beta\approx 0.468. Outside the shaded strips, any c1c_{1} above this maximum, such as 129≈0.03448\frac{1}{29}\approx 0.03448, therefore makes νc1\nu_{c_{1}} an upper bound for all α<β\alpha<\beta. Over α,β≥1\alpha,\beta\geq 1, the surface lies between 0.03180.0318, at α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1, and 8405\frac{8}{405}, approached as α→∞\alpha\to\infty with β/α→∞\beta/\alpha\to\infty; along the diagonal it decreases toward 145\frac{1}{45}.

The small-c∗c^{*} end.

Toward the axes, c∗c^{*} falls to zero, but this part of the surface does not point to useful approximations. For small α\alpha, the median is extremely small, roughly like 2−1/α2^{-1/\alpha}, so an exact ratio form needs gc1​(α)≈0g_{c_{1}}(\alpha)\approx 0.

6 Other choices of c1c_{1}

The minimax value of c1c_{1} over 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta is 0.027537≈1/36.310.027537\approx 1/36.31, with worst relative error 0.189%0.189\% (Table 1). It depends slightly on the error measure: minimizing the worst logit error instead gives 0.027996≈1/35.720.027996\approx 1/35.72, and minimizing the worst deviation |Iνc1​(α,β)−12||I_{\nu_{c_{1}}}(\alpha,\beta)-\frac{1}{2}| of the beta distribution function at the approximation gives 0.027578≈1/36.260.027578\approx 1/36.26. So 136\frac{1}{36} lies within the range of these minimax values. In terms of Figure 2, each minimax value corresponds to the contour of c∗c^{*} that balances the worst errors on its two sides.

Extending the domain below α=1\alpha=1 pushes the minimax value of c1c_{1} up: over α≥12\alpha\geq\frac{1}{2} it is 0.031403≈1/31.840.031403\approx 1/31.84, with worst error 1.05%1.05\%, and over α≥13\alpha\geq\frac{1}{3} it is 0.032615≈1/30.660.032615\approx 1/30.66, with worst error 2.44%2.44\%, attained at α=13\alpha=\frac{1}{3}, both near β=2​α\beta=2\alpha and as β→∞\beta\to\infty. Below α=13\alpha=\frac{1}{3}, no single c1c_{1} does well.

A second coefficient can do somewhat better for larger α\alpha: the series (4) truncated after its c2c_{2} term has worst error 0.167%0.167\% over α≥1\alpha\geq 1, but 3.3%3.3\% over α≥12\alpha\geq\frac{1}{2} and 30%30\% over α≥13\alpha\geq\frac{1}{3}, and lacks the simple factored form.

In the upper right quadrant of Figure 2, where α,β≥1\alpha,\beta\geq 1, c∗c^{*} decreases as α\alpha and β\beta grow, and most of that decrease goes with 1/α+1/β1/\alpha+1/\beta, which suggests letting c1c_{1} depend on that sum. For example, c1=8405+18425515​(1α+1β)c_{1}=\frac{8}{405}+\frac{184}{25515}\big(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}\big), which as β→∞\beta\to\infty reproduces the gamma median expansion (4) through its x−2x^{-2} term, has worst relative error 0.070%0.070\% over 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta, a third of that of ν1/36\nu_{1/36}, and the simpler c1=(3+1/α+1/β)/150c_{1}=(3+1/\alpha+1/\beta)/150 has 0.041%0.041\%, a fifth. The result is no longer of the form g⁡(α)/(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)), since c1c_{1}, and with it each of g⁡(α)g(\alpha) and g⁡(β)g(\beta), depends on both α\alpha and β\beta, and both choices are much worse below α=1\alpha=1, where c1c_{1} grows like 1/α1/\alpha.

7 Gamma median approximation

Each gc1g_{c_{1}} is itself an approximation to the gamma median: it agrees with the expansion (4) in its first two terms, α−13\alpha-\frac{1}{3}, and differs from it by O⁡(1/α)O(1/\alpha). Our recommended member is

g1/36​(α)=(α−16)2α=α−13+136​α.g_{1/36}(\alpha)=\frac{(\alpha-\frac{1}{6})^{2}}{\alpha}=\alpha-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{36\alpha}\,. (6)

By (4), g1/36​(α)−νΓ​(α)∼(136−8405)/α=13/(1620​α)g_{1/36}(\alpha)-\nu_{\Gamma}(\alpha)\sim\big(\frac{1}{36}-\frac{8}{405}\big)/\alpha=13/(1620\,\alpha), so it is an upper bound for large α\alpha. Numerically it is an upper bound for all α>0.7959\alpha>0.7959, where it crosses νΓ\nu_{\Gamma}, and for α≥1\alpha\geq 1 it overestimates by at most 0.212%0.212\%, at α≈1.18\alpha\approx 1.18. At α=1\alpha=1, it gives 2536\frac{25}{36} in place of log⁡2\log 2, 0.19%0.19\% high.

Figure 3 compares it with νΓ\nu_{\Gamma}, with the lower bound α−13\alpha-\frac{1}{3}, and with the upper bound α−13+c1/α\alpha-\frac{1}{3}+c_{1}/\alpha with c1≈0.03194c_{1}\approx 0.03194 described below, for 0<α≤430<\alpha\leq\frac{4}{3}. Above about α=12\alpha=\frac{1}{2}, it is hard to distinguish from the median. Below, its double zero at α=16\alpha=\frac{1}{6} gives a soft parabolic floor, where the true median, roughly like 2−1/α2^{-1/\alpha}, flattens toward zero. A larger c1c_{1} lifts the floor: numerically, the smallest c1c_{1} for which α−13+c1/α≥νΓ​(α)\alpha-\frac{1}{3}+c_{1}/\alpha\geq\nu_{\Gamma}(\alpha) for all α>0\alpha>0 is c1≈0.03194c_{1}\approx 0.03194, for which the two touch near α≈0.294\alpha\approx 0.294. For small shape parameters, where the median behaves like 2−1/α2^{-1/\alpha}, bounds and approximations built around that factor do much better (Lyon,, 2021; Lyon,, 2023).

8 Numerical methods and use of AI tools

Medians were computed with the double-precision inverse incomplete beta and gamma functions of SciPy (Virtanen et al.,, 2020). For each lower limit α0\alpha_{0} of Table 1, worst errors were taken over α0≤α≤1000\alpha_{0}\leq\alpha\leq 1000 (400 logarithmically spaced values) and 1≤β/α≤1051\leq\beta/\alpha\leq 10^{5} (400 values), with β≤106\beta\leq 10^{6}, together with the limit β→∞\beta\to\infty computed from the gamma median. The minimax values of c1c_{1} were found by bounded scalar minimization of the worst error on this grid. The pointwise comparison with Kerman’s approximation used a grid denser near α=13\alpha=\frac{1}{3} and near the diagonal: 400400 linearly spaced values of α\alpha from 13+10−4\frac{1}{3}+10^{-4} to 0.60.6 and 400400 logarithmically spaced values from 0.60.6 to 10001000; 6060 values of β/α\beta/\alpha with β/α−1\beta/\alpha-1 logarithmically spaced from 10−610^{-6} to 10−110^{-1} and 300300 logarithmically spaced from 1.11.1 to 10610^{6}; and β≤106\beta\leq 10^{6}. Near the diagonal at large α\alpha, where both errors approach rounding level, the comparison was confirmed at selected points in 40-digit arithmetic with mpmath (The mpmath development team,, 2026), as was the threshold in Remark 1. A Python notebook that reproduces the figures and the numbers quoted here is included as an ancillary file with the arXiv version of this paper.

This note is a spin-off from a longer manuscript on bounds for the beta median, which the author wrote, including most of its proofs, initially without AI tools; in later work on that manuscript, ChatGPT (OpenAI) was useful in exposing errors in candidate proofs. In preparing the note, the author used Claude (Anthropic) to help refactor and condense material from that manuscript, to check algebra symbolically and numerically, and to port the author’s Matlab scripts to the Python notebook. Claude and Gemini (Google) were used to search for workable proof methods, to check and assess two independently derived sets of proofs, and to synthesize the best of both into Appendix A. Google’s Deep Review tool (Google Research,, 2026) reviewed several generations of the manuscript. The author checked the proofs, revised the text throughout, and is responsible for its content. All numbers quoted can be reproduced from the notebook.

9 Summary

Replacing Kerman’s g⁡(x)=x−13g(x)=x-\frac{1}{3} by g⁡(x)=(x−16)2/xg(x)=(x-\frac{1}{6})^{2}/x, that is, adding 1/(36​x)1/(36x), keeps the ratio form simple, symmetric and exact on the diagonal, and reduces the worst relative error over 1≤α≤β1\leq\alpha\leq\beta from 3.8%3.8\% to 0.21%0.21\%. Numerically on our grid, and asymptotically by Theorem 2, the new approximation is more accurate than Kerman’s wherever the latter is defined, with at most 1332\frac{13}{32} of its error. Theorem 1 places c1=136c_{1}=\frac{1}{36} above the threshold 145\frac{1}{45} for an asymptotic upper bound on every ray, the ideal-parameter map of Section 5 shows where it overestimates and underestimates, and the same gg approximates the gamma median within 0.212%0.212\% for shape parameter at least 11. For posteriors under Kerman’s neutral prior, the member c1≈0.0326c_{1}\approx 0.0326 keeps the relative error within 2.44%2.44\% over the extended domain 13≤α≤β\frac{1}{3}\leq\alpha\leq\beta.

Appendix A Proofs

A.1 The median logit

The proofs work with the logit, logit⁡p=log⁡(p/(1−p))\logit p=\log(p/(1-p)), of the median. Three properties make it convenient. Because the logit is increasing, it maps the median of a distribution on (0,1)(0,1) to the median of the transformed distribution: logit⁡νB​(α,β)\logit\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta) is the median of logit⁡X\logit X for X∼Beta⁡(α,β)X\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta), whose density is smooth and log-concave on the whole real line. The logit of a ratio form separates into a difference, logit⁡(g⁡(α)/(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β)))=log⁡g⁡(α)−log⁡g⁡(β)\logit\big(g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(\beta))\big)=\log g(\alpha)-\log g(\beta), so it can be compared with the median one shape parameter at a time. And the symmetry νB​(β,α)=1−νB​(α,β)\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\beta,\alpha)=1-\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta) becomes a change of sign, with logit⁡νB=0\logit\nu_{\mathrm{B}}=0 on the diagonal.

Write Δ=1/α−1/β\Delta=1/\alpha-1/\beta, a measure of the departure from the diagonal: it is zero there and positive for α<β\alpha<\beta. Along a ray β=r​α\beta=r\alpha, we have Δ=(1−1/r)/α\Delta=(1-1/r)/\alpha, so approximations to the logit of the median can be ordered by powers of 1/α1/\alpha. We use three, of orders 00, 11 and 22:

L0​(α,β)\displaystyle L_{0}(\alpha,\beta) =log⁡αβ,L1​(α,β)=L0​(α,β)−Δ3,\displaystyle=\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\,,\qquad L_{1}(\alpha,\beta)=L_{0}(\alpha,\beta)-\frac{\Delta}{3}\,,
L2​(α,β)\displaystyle L_{2}(\alpha,\beta) =L1​(α,β)−Δ⁡(29​α2+50​α​β+29​β2)810​α​β​(α+β).\displaystyle=L_{1}(\alpha,\beta)-\frac{\Delta\,(29\alpha^{2}+50\alpha\beta+29\beta^{2})}{810\,\alpha\beta\,(\alpha+\beta)}\,. (7)

The zeroth, L0L_{0}, is the logit of the mean α/(α+β)\alpha/(\alpha+\beta). The first, L1L_{1}, agrees to first order with the logit of Kerman’s approximation, log⁡(α−13)−log⁡(β−13)=L1+O⁡(α−2)\log(\alpha-\frac{1}{3})-\log(\beta-\frac{1}{3})=L_{1}+O(\alpha^{-2}), which is why that approximation is correct to first order. The second, L2L_{2}, adds the second-order correction that decides the bounds of Theorem 1. Lemma 1 shows that it matches the logit of the median to second order; its coefficients come out of Laplace’s method in the proof.

Lemma 1 (Large-shape expansion).

Fix r≥1r\geq 1. As α→∞\alpha\to\infty with β=r​α\beta=r\alpha,

logit⁡νB​(α,β)=L2​(α,β)+O⁡(α−3).\logit\nu_{\mathrm{B}}(\alpha,\beta)=L_{2}(\alpha,\beta)+O(\alpha^{-3})\,. (8)
Proof.

Let n=α+βn=\alpha+\beta, p=α/np=\alpha/n and q=β/nq=\beta/n, which are fixed along the ray.
